description: Uzay, bilim, yazılım ve yapay zekâyı bir araya getirerek geleceğin keşif teknolojilerini geliştirmeyi hedefliyoruz. Bu yıl Mars yüzeyine ait bilimsel verilerle arazi koşullarını analiz eden, güvenli rotaların belirlenmesine yardımcı olan ve gelecekteki astronotların keşiflerini destekleyen akıllı bir harita sistemi geliştirmeyi amaçlıyoruz. Ekibimizde merak eden, araştıran, yeni fikirler üretmekten çekinmeyen ve birlikte öğrenmeye açık insanlara yer veriyoruz
summary: Mars Hazard Map is a browser-based interactive 3D globe that shows hazards on the Martian surface and calculates the safest and fastest route between two points. Each route becomes step-by-step navigation for either a pressurized rover or an astronaut on foot. The project keeps real data (MOLA elevation, documented event sites, real landing attempts, Curiosity radiation measurements, and Mars24 solar position) clearly separate from models with openly stated formulas (hazard score, temperature, pressure, landing suitability, and route cost). A companion Python analysis of 4,745 days of Curiosity weather data and 3,297 days of Viking pressure data produced findings such as an 11.26 km scale height and the 2018 dust storm narrowing Gale Crater’s day-night temperature swing from 69 °C to 50 °C. We used these results to recalibrate the models. Future crewed missions will need hazard and route information that is trustworthy and easy to read. This tool brings NASA data together in one place that anyone can open in a browser, and it is honest about what is measured and what is modeled.
details:
Introduction and purpose

The Martian surface poses four basic hazards to an astronaut: radiation, extreme cold, rugged terrain, and dust storms. Curiosity's RAD instrument measured an average surface dose of about 0.64 mSv per day [4, 20]. The 2018 global dust storm ended the Opportunity rover [26, 27], and Phoenix was lost during the polar winter [35, 36].

In NASA's crewed Mars plans, the area around a landing site is defined as an "Exploration Zone" with a radius of about 100 km [10]. This creates a need for detailed information at distances the crew can cover by vehicle or on foot.

Today this information is scattered across many sources: elevation datasets, mission reports, scientific papers, and news. The project aims to combine them on a single screen and to show real data separately from estimates.

Project goals:

  • Show Mars as a rotatable 3D globe embossed with real elevation.
  • When the pointer is over a location, show the astronaut hazard level there and the real event that took place there, together with its source.
  • When two points are selected, calculate the safest and the fastest route, and give the risk of the fast route as well.
  • Provide information at the 100 km close-up scale, at distances people can actually travel.
  • Provide step-by-step navigation for a pressurized rover and for an astronaut on foot, taking into account the Sun, duration, dose, and dust season.
  • Show the real rocket landing sites and the regions suitable for a safe landing.
  • Download and clean real measurements from Mars, organize them by date and location, calculate averages, maxima, and minima, and examine the changes with charts.

Data sources

Every real value on the map is based on a published source. The page does not fetch live data; all data is embedded in the page. The numbers in square brackets correspond to the References.

Data rule: Only data from NASA and from the partner agencies of NASA Space Apps is used in the project. The partner agencies include ESA, CSA, JAXA, ISRO, ASI, AEE (Spain), MBRSC, and the Turkish Space Agency (TUA).

The data in this project comes from NASA and ESA; Curiosity's weather station REMS is Spain's contribution to NASA. No Mars dataset published by TUA was found for this work. News sites and encyclopedias are not used as sources.

The ten documented event sites and their records:

  • Gale Crater (Curiosity): In the September 2017 solar storm, surface radiation rose to more than twice the highest value measured since landing [12].
  • Jezero Crater (Perseverance): At least four dust devils pass on a typical Martian day; in the regional dust storm of January 2022, sand damaged the wind sensors [23–25].
  • Meridiani Planum (Opportunity): Contact was lost in the 2018 global dust storm, and the rover was declared lost in February 2019 [26, 27].
  • Schiaparelli impact site (ESA): On 19 October 2016, the lander hit the surface at about 540 km/h [30, 31].
  • Gusev Crater (Spirit): On 1 May 2009, it got stuck in soft soil near Home Plate; last contact was on 22 March 2010 [32, 33].
  • Elysium Planitia (InSight): Power ran out because dust accumulated on the panels; the mission ended on 21 December 2022 [22, 34].
  • Vastitas Borealis (Phoenix): The 2008 polar winter cut off the light; last contact was on 2 November 2008 [35, 36].
  • Utopia Planitia (Zhurong): HiRISE images showed that the rover did not move at all between September 2022 and February 2023 [37, 38].
  • Olympus Mons: In the 2018 global storm, the summit stayed above the dust [29].
  • Hellas Planitia: The lowest mapped region; there is no verified event record for it in this study [5].

Method

The application is a single HTML file and performs its calculations in the browser, even without an internet connection. The 3D rendering uses the three.js (r128) library [40]; the calculations are done in plain JavaScript.

Real data is in the left column; the models in the middle column calculate only from this data, and the results appear in the map features in the right column.

1. 3D globe and texture alignment

The globe was taken from the USDZ Mars model provided for the project. The model contains a cube-sphere mesh and a texture of 2048 × 1536 pixels, but it has no latitude-longitude information.

The texture was compared with the known locations of the Olympus Mons caldera and the Hellas basin. The real longitude was found to be 180° more than the longitude in the model, and this rotation was applied to the corners of the mesh. The alignment was later checked against the MOLA elevation contours at Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, and Hellas; the difference is less than half a degree.

The model's 2,034 vertices were subdivided three times to about 100,000 vertices. Each vertex is pushed up or down by the real MOLA elevation. The relief is exaggerated 8× by default and can be adjusted between 1× and 30×.

2. Real elevation calculation

Elevation was calculated from two real models. MarsTopo719 is the Mars shape (radius) model, derived from MOLA measurements [5] and given by spherical harmonic coefficients up to degree 719 [8]. GMM-3 is the gravity model derived from MGS, Mars Odyssey, and MRO radio tracking [2].

MOLA's zero level is the equipotential surface called the "areoid". The potential of this surface was found iteratively so that the mean equatorial radius is 3396.000 km. The result was 12,652,804.4 m²/s², which is very close to the 12,652,804.7 m²/s² value used by MOLA. Mars's rotation rate was taken as 7.088218 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s.

The calculation was done on a 0.125° grid with the pyshtools library [7], then downsampled to a 0.25° grid of 721 × 1440 nodes. Values were rounded to whole meters. Each value was predicted from its left, upper, and upper-left neighbors and only the difference was stored (zigzag varint), compressing the data to 1.8 MB.

In the browser, elevation is read with Catmull–Rom bicubic interpolation so that it does not look blocky. Slope is calculated from central differences with a base of about 30 km.

3. Hazard model

The hazard score is the weighted sum of four components; each component takes a value between 0 and 1.

Extra points are added to a location where a documented event took place, and this is shown in the panel. The score is divided into four levels: below 24 is "relatively low", 24–34 is "medium", 34–44 is "high", and 44 and above is "very high". "Relatively low" does not mean safe, because no place on Mars is close to occupational dose limits on Earth.

4. Temperature and pressure

The temperature model was anchored to the ground temperature measured by Curiosity's REMS station at Gale between 2012 and 2026 [42, 43]. The average of the daily maximum ground temperature is +2.8 °C, and the average of the nightly minimum is −81.5 °C. Mean temperature changes with latitude as a cosine and with elevation at about −2.5 °C/km. In the first versions, the model was anchored to press reports about Perseverance's measurements at Jezero; because of the data rule, it was switched to NASA data.

Both constants of the pressure model were found from Curiosity and Viking measurements in the Mars Data Analysis System (details below). The first versions used the textbook values of 6.1 mbar and 11.1 km.

5. Landing suitability

The hard limits were taken from NASA's engineering guide for the Curiosity (MSL) landing site [11]: latitude between 60°N and 60°S, elevation at most +2 km, and slope at most 3°. A place that exceeds any of these limits is considered "not suitable".

Places that pass the limits get a score between 0 and 100. Lower places get a higher score, because a thick atmosphere helps the rocket brake; InSight asked for a site below −2.5 km [3].

Each factor is clipped to between 0 and 1. A score of 65 and above is considered "good", and 40–65 is considered "marginal".

6. Route planning

On the globe, routes are calculated on a grid of 161 × 360 nodes at 1° spacing (about 59 km), covering 80°N to 80°S. The Dijkstra algorithm runs with a binary heap. Each node is connected to 16 neighbors; because knight-move directions are included, the route does not zigzag like a staircase.

The safe route uses a cost that makes risky segments more expensive by the square of the risk. The fast route only minimizes time; vehicle speed falls as slope increases.

Here L is the edge length (km), u is the average risk score at the two ends of the edge divided by 100, and e is the slope. On the 100 km close-up map, the same method runs on a 117 × 117 grid with 2 km spacing. The safe route is then turned into a smooth line with Douglas–Peucker simplification and three rounds of Chaikin smoothing.

7. Navigation simulation

When a route is selected, the trip is simulated over time in 15-minute steps. If "Move only in daylight" is on, the vehicle waits in 10-minute steps while the Sun is below the horizon. If the Sun does not rise for more than two days, the route is considered to have entered polar night and a warning is given.

  • Pressurized rover: The speed of about 10 km/h from the NASA SEV fact sheet is used [9]. If the path exceeds 200 km, an intermediate base or resupply warning is given, because the two-vehicle range in the SEV plan is exceeded.
  • Astronaut on foot: A walking speed of 3 km/h on flat ground and an 8-hour EVA are assumed. If the one-way time does not exceed 4 hours, the astronaut can go and return in a single EVA; if it exceeds 8 hours, a trip on foot is not possible.
  • Dose: The time spent on the surface during the trip is multiplied by the daily dose of about 0.64 mSv measured by RAD [4]. Vehicle shielding is not taken into account.
  • Dust season: The season (Ls) is tracked throughout the trip. If it enters the Ls 185–315° range, a global storm warning is given; if it is within Ls 180–360°, a dusty season warning is given [6].
  • Directions: The route is simplified with Douglas–Peucker and the remaining vertices become turn points. A heading change under 12° is written as "continue straight", up to 35° as "slight", and over 120° as "sharp" turn.
  • Elevation profile: MOLA elevation is sampled along the route at up to 2,000 points; total and per-step climb and descent are calculated.
  • Voice directions: Each new step is read aloud in Turkish using the browser's speech feature (Web Speech API).

8. Day-night and Sun position

The point where the Sun is directly overhead is calculated from the real date and time with NASA GISS's Mars24 algorithm [1]. The algorithm uses the Mars Sun date, mean anomaly, planetary perturbations, the season angle (Ls), the equation of time, and Mars mean time.

From this point, the local solar time, the Sun's elevation, and its direction are found for every place. The light on the globe comes from this direction, and the dark face shows the real night. By speeding up time, the user can watch a Martian day in about 40 seconds.

9. 100 km close-up map

The close-up map covers 116 km around the selected point and can be zoomed in up to 40×. When the "100 km close-up map" button is pressed, the camera descends toward that point on the globe, and then the close-up map opens smoothly.

In the default "Mars surface" view, the colors are the same as on the globe. The globe's texture is drawn from directly above that region, unlit, with an orthographic camera on the graphics card. On top of these colors, relief shading calculated from MOLA and contour lines drawn with the marching squares method are added.

The map is drawn with the same detail at every scale. The visible area is sampled at every moment with a grid whose cells correspond to about 4.5 pixels on screen; when zooming or panning, the grid is rebuilt immediately, and it never falls back to a coarse grid. The contour interval also shrinks with scale: for example, the 500 m interval at Gale in the 100 km view becomes 50 m after zooming in 10×. This way, the density of lines on screen stays the same at every zoom level.

When navigation starts, the map switches to a Google Maps style. The map rotates according to the vehicle's heading and is shown tilted with CSS 3D transforms. The green banner at the top shows the next turn and its distance; the bottom shows remaining time, distance, arrival time, and dose.

10. Real sky, moons, and Mars clock

The sky behind the globe is drawn with real data. 12,495 stars brighter than magnitude 6.8 are taken from ESA's Hipparcos catalogue [52]. Each star's position, brightness, and color come from the catalogue.

The stars' directions are first found in the celestial equatorial system (ICRF), then converted to Mars's body frame. For this conversion, Mars's pole direction and its current rotation angle are used; both come from the IAU 2000 constants of NASA JPL NAIF [53]. In this way, Mars's real sky at that moment is seen on screen.

Phobos and Deimos always keep the same face toward Mars in their orbits. Because the IAU constants give the orientation of these faces, the longitude of the moons as seen from Mars is found as W_moon + 180° − W_Mars [53]. The orbital radii are taken from NASA NSSDCA: Phobos 9,378 km, Deimos 23,459 km [54]. The bodies are drawn 4–6 times larger so that they are visible.

The direction and distance of Earth from Mars are calculated from the orbital elements given by JPL for 1800–2050 [55]. The label shows the distance in AU and the time light takes to travel from Earth to Mars.

The Mars clock in the top bar comes from the Mars24 algorithm [1]: Coordinated Mars Time (MTC), Mars Sol Date (MSD), Mars year [47], and season (Ls). At startup, the camera approaches Mars from a distance; when the user touches the screen, this motion stops immediately.

Mars Data Analysis System

The map's hazard model estimates temperature and pressure with formulas anchored to a single measurement (Jezero). This part of the project, in contrast, works directly with data measured on the surface of Mars. The goal is to download and clean real measurements, organize them by date and location, calculate basic statistics, and examine the changes with charts.

The analysis was done in Python: pandas for tables [49], NumPy for calculations [50], and Matplotlib for charts [51]. The script is named mars_veri_analizi.py. Its output, the clean data, was embedded in the "Data analysis" panel on the map. For the selected date range, the panel recalculates the same statistics in the browser and draws the charts interactively.

When NASA's servers cannot be reached, the script uses a byte-for-byte copy of the same raw files on GitHub [48]. The address used and the SHA-256 digest of each file are recorded, so that which data the analysis used can be verified later.

Steps

  1. Download: The REMS feed (JSON), the drive points (GeoJSON), the Viking data, and the PDS label are downloaded.
    • In REMS, missing values were written as "--"; these were converted to missing data (NaN) and text numbers were converted to numbers.
    • The humidity and wind columns were empty in all 4,745 records and were dropped.
    • The data was checked for duplicate sols, values outside the physical range (e.g. pressure outside 300–1300 Pa), and days when the nightly temperature was higher than the daytime one; none were found.
    • Finally, isolated measurements deviating by more than 6 times the local MAD (at least 18 units) from a 15-sol rolling median were removed.
    • The Viking file is a fixed-width text table. Columns were read using the start byte and length definitions in the PDS label, −9.999 flags were counted as missing, and millibars were converted to pascals.
  2. Organize: Each measurement was given an Earth date, a Mars year (MY), and a Mars month (a 30° slice of Ls). Mars years follow the numbering of Clancy et al. [47]: Curiosity landed in MY 31 and the Vikings in MY 12. For location, each sol was given the latitude, longitude, and elevation of the last drive point where Curiosity was on that day. For the Viking data, the date was calculated as the number of sols since landing × 1.0275 days.
  3. Analyze: For each measurement, the mean, standard deviation, and the maximum and minimum values with their dates were calculated. Group statistics were also produced by Mars year, Mars month, and 100 m elevation band. For the effect of location, the model below was fitted with the NumPy least squares method, where z is elevation (km) and L is the season angle (Ls).

1. Mars's atmosphere "breathes" every year. At all three landing sites, pressure falls and rises in the same seasons. The lowest value is around Ls 145–155°: toward the end of winter in the southern hemisphere, when the south polar cap is largest. The highest value is around Ls 255°: at the end of southern spring, as the cap melts and turns back into gas. The cause is that carbon dioxide freezes at the winter pole and returns to gas in spring [46]. In 10° seasonal averages, the lowest value is 20% below the highest at Gale, 23% at Viking 1, and 25% at Viking 2. In other words, roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of the atmosphere freezes and thaws at the poles every year. The north pole also creates a second, smaller fluctuation: a second peak around Ls 50° and a second trough around Ls 330°.

Pressure by season (Matplotlib output, chart 02): pressure is lowest around Ls 150 and highest around Ls 255 for Curiosity, Viking 1, and Viking 2. Points are daily values and lines are 10° Ls averages. Viking 2's variation is the largest; it is the landing site closest to the north polar cap.

2. The long-term decline in pressure comes from location, not climate. At Gale, the annual mean pressure fell from 841.9 Pa in MY 32 to 796.5 Pa in MY 37. This means a drop of about 9.3 Pa per Mars year. But in the same period, Curiosity climbed 1,019 m up Mount Sharp (from −4,521 m to −3,502 m). Elevation and season together explain 99.6% of the variation in daily pressure (R² = 0.996). The calculated scale height is H = 11.26 km; that is, pressure decreases by a factor of e (≈2.7) for every 11.26 km of climb. The expected value for Mars is about 11 km. Once the seasonal effect is removed, almost all of the remaining long-term decline is explained by the climb. In other words, this data shows no sign that the atmosphere has been thinning over the years.

Left: Curiosity's elevation rises from −4,500 m to −3,500 m between 2012 and 2026. Right: in full Mars years, annual mean pressure falls as elevation rises (Matplotlib output, chart 04). The trend on the right was calculated only from Mars years covering all seasons (MY 32–37).

3. The 2018 global dust storm suppressed Gale's daily cycle. June–August 2018 (Ls 185–240) was compared with the same season in the other seven Mars years:

  • The day-night difference fell from 69.1 °C to 50.4 °C.
  • The daytime maximum temperature fell from 0 °C to −15.1 °C, and the maximum ground temperature fell from +12.4 °C to −4.6 °C.
  • The nightly minimum temperature, on the other hand, rose from −69.0 °C to −65.5 °C.

Dust in the air blocked sunlight during the day and radiated heat at night. The smallest day-night difference in the entire record (31 °C, 20 June 2018) and the coldest ground day (−24 °C, 3 July 2018) are within this storm. The same storm ended Opportunity's mission at the Meridiani Planum point on the map [26, 27].

4. The daily temperature swing at Gale is very large. The daytime maximum air temperature averages −12 °C and the nightly minimum −74 °C; the difference between them averages 62 °C every day. Days are coolest around Ls 85° (average −27 °C) and warmest around Ls 215° (average −1 °C). After these measurements, the map's temperature model was anchored to the REMS ground temperature at Gale: the model now gives +2.7 °C by day and −81.5 °C by night for Gale. The previous model, since it was anchored to press reports about Jezero, gave +14 °C and −76 °C for the same place.

5. The map's pressure model was recalibrated with measurements. The previous model used 6.1 mbar at zero level and a scale height of 11.1 km. This model gave 9.0 mbar for Gale, whereas Curiosity measured an annual mean of 8.0–8.4 mbar there. The season-free annual pressure of each landing site was carried to zero level using its own MOLA elevation. The results came out close to each other:

  • Gale: 5.67 mbar
  • Viking 1: 5.75 mbar
  • Viking 2: 5.84 mbar

The average of the three values is 5.75 mbar. The map's pressure layer and information panel now use P = 5.75 · e^(−h / 11.26) mbar. In this way, both constants of the model come from NASA measurements.

Interface and usage

The screen has two parts: the 3D globe on the left and the information panel on the right. On a phone, the panel moves below the globe.

Globe

  • It is rotated with the mouse or a finger and zoomed with the wheel or two fingers. If it is not touched for a while, it slowly rotates by itself.
  • Keyboard: the arrow keys rotate, + and − zoom, Enter opens the point in the center, and Esc stops navigation or closes an open window.
  • Nine layers: real surface, elevation/depth, slope, daytime temperature, night cold, pressure, radiation, hazard, and landing suitability. Under each layer, the color scale and whether the data is real or a model are written.
  • There are options for a relief exaggeration slider, a latitude-longitude grid, and turning landing markers on and off.
  • In the background, the ESA Hipparcos stars, the orbits of Phobos and Deimos, and Earth are visible. Zooming out with the wheel lets you watch the whole moon system.
  • In the top bar, the Mars clock (MTC), Mars Sol Date, Mars year, and season are continuously updated. The "Data sources" button shows each dataset with its agency and link.
  • The Sun box shows the current season (Ls), the point where the Sun is overhead, and the dust season. The "Now", "Speed up time", and "Day/night" buttons are here.

Points and information panel

  • The colored circles are the documented event sites; the color shows the hazard level. A short note appears on hover and the details open on click.
  • The detail panel contains the hazard score and its components, the real event, measurements, MOLA elevation and slope, model temperature and pressure, landing suitability, local solar time, and numbered sources.
  • The diamond markers are the real landing sites: white is successful, orange landed but the mission ended, gray failed, and purple is a SpaceX Starship candidate.
  • Clicking anywhere on the globe also opens the information for that point.

Route and navigation

  • The start (A) and destination (B) are chosen from the panel, from the list, or by clicking on the globe. The "Pressurized rover" or "Astronaut (on foot)" profile is selected.
  • The safest route is drawn in blue and the fastest route in pink. For each, the distance, travel time, total time including waits for night, dose, average and highest risk, and the riskiest place are given.
  • The navigation card has departure and arrival local time, climb and descent, dust warning, elevation profile, and step-by-step directions with arrow icons.
  • With "Start navigation", the vehicle moves along the route, the camera follows it, and the day-night line shifts according to simulation time. Speed can be 1×, 2×, or 4×; voice directions can be turned on.

100 km close-up map

  • You can switch between "Mars surface" (the colors on the globe), "Map (light)", and eight data layers.
  • The point clicked on the map becomes the destination. The blue selected route and gray alternative route, time bubbles, a red destination pin, and direction arrows on the route are shown.
  • With "Start", Google Maps style navigation opens: a tilted map that turns with the heading, a blue vehicle arrow, a green turn banner, and a bottom info bar.
  • Nearby real records and InSight's real landing ellipse (130 × 27 km) [3] are shown on the map.

Data analysis

It is opened with the "Mars data analysis" button in the panel, or with the button in the information panel of the Gale, Curiosity, Viking 1, and Viking 2 points.

Three choices are made:

  1. Landing site.
  2. Measurement: pressure, nightly and daytime air temperature, ground temperature, or day-night difference.
  3. Grouping: Mars year, Mars month, Earth year, or elevation band.

The date range can also be narrowed. For the selected range, the following are calculated: mean, maximum and minimum values (with their dates), standard deviation, and the number of valid records. When the whole period is selected, it also states that the results are the same as the Python output.

There are three charts:

  • Time series, with a 30-sol moving average.
  • Seasonal cycle, compared with the other landing sites.
  • Group statistics.

For Curiosity, a season-free pressure–elevation chart and the scale height calculation are also shown. The "2018 global dust storm" button opens the storm period and compares its effect with other years.

The selected profile, day-night setting, layer, sound, and speed are remembered in the browser.

Limitations

The map is not a mission planning tool; it is an educational and exploration tool fed with real data. Which value is real and which is a model is written next to every value on the page.

Real data

Model or assumption

MOLA elevation, slope, and contour lines

Hazard score and its four components

Event dates, measurements, and their sources

Temperature (anchored to the REMS measurement at Gale) and pressure (tuned to the measurements of three landing sites)

Landing coordinates and outcomes

Landing suitability score

Sun position and season (Mars24)

Route cost and slope-dependent speed reduction

Daily dose measured by RAD

Walking speed (3 km/h) and EVA duration (8 h)

SEV rover speed and range

Ignoring vehicle shielding in the dose calculation

REMS and Viking measurements

Outlier threshold (6 MAD, at least 18 units) and the pressure model using a single global constant

  • Resolution: Elevation is at 15 km and the texture at about 10 km resolution. Smaller craters, rocks, sand fields, and slopes are not visible. The close-up map keeps its on-screen detail at every scale, but this is denser sampling of the same 15 km data; no new craters or rocks appear when zooming in. No made-up detail was added.
  • No live data: The page does not fetch live weather, dust, or radiation data from the internet. The Sun position is calculated live, but it is an astronomical calculation, not a measurement.
  • Slope scale: Slope is measured with a base of about 30 km. For this reason, even a flat landing site with a large mountain nearby, like Gale, can be rated "high hazard".
  • Landing suitability: The 5 m and 2–5 km scale slope and rock density criteria in the MSL guide are not in this data. The score is only a preliminary screen.
  • Routes: There are no roads on Mars. The blue line is not a road; it is a recommended transit corridor calculated from the terrain and the model.
  • Estimated locations: The landing coordinates of Mars 2, Mars 6, and Mars Polar Lander are estimates; the panel states this.
  • REMS feed: The REMS data used is the publicly available daily summary of the Centro de Astrobiología; the scientifically calibrated raw data is in the REMS products at PDS. Measurement hours vary from sol to sol, so the daily minimum and maximum values belong only to the hours when measurements were made. Humidity and wind are not published in this feed.
  • Viking data: Viking 2's daily pressure record ends in August 1979; the second Mars year is not complete. This dataset has no temperature.
  • Pressure calibration: The three landing sites lie between 48°N and 5°S. In polar regions, real pressure may deviate from the model, because the scale height is smaller in cold air.
  • Moon and Earth positions: Phobos and Deimos are drawn 4–6 times larger; Deimos's 1.8° orbital inclination is not shown. Earth's position is calculated from approximate orbital elements; this is accurate enough for the purpose of this page.
  • Zhurong: The China National Space Administration (CNSA) is not a NASA Space Apps partner agency. For this reason, the record of Zhurong is based only on NASA's HiRISE images.
  • Texture alignment: The 3D model's texture is aligned to better than half a degree; even so, at the 100 km scale there may be a shift of tens of kilometers between the colors and the contour lines.

Development process

The project developed over fourteen versions. Each version responded to a gap noticed in the previous version or to a new need.

The most important turning point is version 9. In the first versions, elevation was a model built from known large features and was off by several km in some places. After switching to real MOLA data, the hazard score, routes, and close-up map sat on real terrain. In version 12, the same approach was applied to weather data: the pressure model is now based on the measurements of three landers instead of a textbook value.

Conclusion and future work

The project combined the hazards on the Martian surface, the real landing history, and route planning on a single browser page. Its strongest aspect is that it shows the source of every value and clearly separates real data from model calculation.

The Mars Data Analysis System revealed what was actually measured in the places the map shows. Gale's 14-year weather record and the Vikings' pressure record from the 1970s show the same seasonal cycle. Both constants of the map's pressure model were found from these measurements.

The switch to real MOLA elevation was the project's biggest quality step. Gale Crater and Mount Sharp, Valles Marineris, and Olympus Mons are now seen in their real shapes, and routes are calculated on this real terrain.

Things that can be done in the future:

  • Finer terrain: HiRISE stereo elevation models (at meter scale) and CTX mosaics can be added to the close-up map. This would make rocks and small slopes visible.
  • Rock and ground data: Rock density and sand fields can be added to the hazard model with THEMIS thermal inertia maps.
  • Water ice: Subsurface ice maps can be added as a resource layer for crewed landing and base site selection.
  • More weather data: Calibrated REMS products at PDS, Perseverance MEDA products, InSight wind measurements, and Pathfinder data can be added to the analysis system. The temperature model is currently anchored only to Gale; with MEDA data, Jezero can be added to build a two-point model.
  • Seasonal hazard: The dust component can be a value that varies by season (Ls) and region instead of a constant.
  • Robotic application: The route and navigation algorithms can be adapted to the path planner of a real rover robot. The same Dijkstra, slope-dependent speed, and night-waiting logic is also useful for terrain robots on Earth.
